sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.markdown: **No state license covers chimney work in Indiana.** The state licenses **plumbers** but has **no statewide general-contractor or home-improvement license** — Indiana leaves that to local governments. What the state imposes is consumer paperwork, not a credential: the home improvement contracts chapter, **Ind. Code 24-5-11**, applies to any "real property improvement contract" whose price **exceeds $150** (IC 24-5-11-4) and prescribes written-contract contents (IC 24-5-11-10: parties, supplier contact info, detailed description, start/completion dates, contract price). Licensing is **LOCAL**: **Indianapolis/Marion County** (Dept. of Business & Neighborhood Services) licenses certain trades; other large cities may run their own registration — **not individually confirmed; do not name Fort Wayne/Evansville programs on the page.** "Licensed and bonded" in Indiana usually means a city registration plus insurance, not a state exam or registry.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: As wide as Ohio's and Illinois's (comparison). Statewide there is **nothing to verify for chimney work** beyond a written contract — no exam, no registry — and local licensing, where it exists, tests general trade/permit knowledge, not flue diagnosis. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) and an independent audit fill a genuine vacuum.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV statute — high; form wording — high, current form read Sep 25, 2026)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: statute — high; form wording — high, current form read Sep 25, 2026
sections.markdown: **Ind. Code 32-21-5** requires the seller of 1–4 unit residential property to complete a disclosure form adopted by the Indiana Real Estate Commission (IC 32-21-5-7), covering the known condition of "the foundation, the mechanical systems, the roof, the structure, the water and sewer systems" and other listed items; the prescribed form is the **Seller's Residential Real Estate Sales Disclosure (State Form 46234)**. **The form changed in 2026.** The Indiana Real Estate Commission adopted an updated form, **State Form 46234 (R9/2-26)**, as a final rule on March 11, 2026 (LSA Document #25-627; in.gov/pla/rulesingov/lsa-document-25-627, checked Sep 25, 2026 — the PLA page does not state the rule's effective date), and R9/2-26 is the version the state forms catalog now serves (forms.in.gov/Download.aspx?id=16805, checked Sep 25, 2026). On R9/2-26, section **1.D "Heating & Cooling System"** lists **"Woodburning Stove," "Fireplace,"** and **"Fireplace Insert"** as rows to mark Not Applicable/Rented, Defective, Not Defective, or Unknown, and section 1.B "Electrical System" has a row for **"Smoke / Fire Alarms Carbon Monoxide Detectors."** **The words "chimney" and "flue" do not appear on R9/2-26.** The older form (R6/6-14) asked "Are the furnace/woodstove/chimney/flue all in working order?" (copy at in.gov/health/eph/files/46234-fill-in.pdf) — that question is **not** on the current form, so the page must not quote it as current. Actual-knowledge basis; the form is not a warranty. No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD. (State Form 46021 is the separate tax "Sales Disclosure" — different document.)

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: The **Deceptive Consumer Sales Act (DCSA), Ind. Code 24-5-0.5**: a consumer relying on an uncured or incurable deceptive act may recover **actual damages or $500, whichever is greater**; for a **willful** act the court may increase damages to **the greater of 3× actual damages or $1,000**, plus attorney's fees (IC 24-5-0.5-4(a)). **Senior consumers (age 60+, IC 24-5-0.5-2) relying on an uncured or incurable deceptive act "may bring an action to recover treble damages, if appropriate" (IC 24-5-0.5-4(i))** — a distinctive Indiana angle for elder chimney-scam targets (treble is available, not automatic). **Violations of the home improvement contracts chapter are deceptive acts actionable by the AG or a consumer under IC 24-5-0.5-4 (IC 24-5-11-14).** Separately, **Home Solicitation Sales (Ind. Code 24-5-10)** give a right to cancel **before midnight of the third business day** after the later of the agreement or the supplier's required notice (IC 24-5-10-8). The Indiana AG's Consumer Protection Division enforces; its home-improvement fact sheet restates "Indiana law requires home improvement contracts exceeding $150 to be in writing," notes "Licensing requirements vary from community to community," and takes complaints at 1-800-382-5516 / IndianaConsumer.com (in.gov/attorneygeneral/consumer-protection-division/files/CPD_Fact_Sheet-Home_improv_Scams.pdf, checked Sep 25, 2026 — GOV).

sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown: Indiana has a **statewide building code** through the **Fire Prevention & Building Safety Commission** — the **2020 Indiana Residential Code, which adopts the 2018 IRC by reference** — enforced by local building departments. IDHS's 2025 readoption review says the Commission is reviewing the latest national model codes for an update, with no adoption date set. The Commission's new **2026 Indiana Building Code** final rule (2024 IBC with Indiana amendments; IDHS posting dated June 1, 2026, in.gov/dhs/files/Building-Code-LSA-Document-6.1.2026.pdf — DOC) covers Class 1 (commercial) structures only and leaves one- and two-family dwellings under the Indiana Residential Code (675 IAC 14); the Indiana Association of Building Officials still lists the 2020 Indiana Residential Code (2018 IRC base, effective Dec 26, 2019) as current (iabo.com/Current-Code, checked Sep 25, 2026 — REF). Chimney relines, rebuilds, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally permit work where local enforcement exists; in some rural/unincorporated areas enforcement is light. Include the local-variance disclaimer.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — high confidence; the weak spot)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **Indiana is the CO laggard of this set.** No statewide CO-alarm mandate for existing 1–2 family dwellings was found. The Indiana Residential Code's **R315** requires CO alarms in dwelling units with a fuel-fired appliance or attached garage for new construction, and IDHS's R315 guidance states: **"Carbon monoxide alarms are not required to be installed in townhouses and one- and two-family dwellings when alterations, repairs or additions occur."** No CO requirement at sale was found — the 2026 seller form (R9/2-26) only asks the seller to mark the condition of any "Smoke / Fire Alarms Carbon Monoxide Detectors" present; it does not require them. Some cities add rental rules (e.g., Bloomington — not re-verified). Absence is the finding: most existing Indiana homes carry no state CO-alarm obligation — a live safety talking point, not a gap to gloss.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime; outdoor wood boilers regulated locally where at all. Not a material content section for IN.

sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The Indiana AG's Consumer Protection Division pursues home-improvement fraud under the DCSA and IC 24-5-11, and the door-knock "we noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook Home Solicitation Sales (24-5-10) + incurable-deceptive-act scenario — with the senior-treble provision especially relevant. **Specific IN chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT CONFIRMED** — patterns, not names.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: Indiana is the **light-touch, CO-laggard** state: no state chimney license (only plumbers are state-licensed), just a written-contract mandate over $150 and the Deceptive Consumer Sales Act behind it — and **no statewide CO-alarm requirement for existing homes found.** It sits in the Ohio/Illinois family (comparison: no state license, local patchwork, real seller disclosure), but with a weaker safety floor and one distinctive lever: the DCSA lets **senior (60+) consumers seek treble damages** for incurable or uncured deceptive acts — aimed squarely at the elder homeowners chimney scammers target. The credential vacuum is the pitch — there's nothing statewide to look up for the person on your roof.
